name: Mirror and Water Images — Flipping Letters, Words and Clocks
whatIsIt: A mirror image flips something left-to-right, exactly like holding it up to a vertical mirror. A water image flips something top-to-bottom, like looking at its reflection in still water below it. Some letters and clock times look identical after flipping; most don't — learning which is which is the whole skill.
whyNeeded: Mirror/water image questions train precise left-right and top-bottom spatial reasoning — recognizing exactly what changes and what stays the same under a flip, a skill used in reading maps, following diagrams, and any visual-spatial task.
realLifeUses: Reasoning sections of SSC, banking and railway exams
Reading a reflection correctly (mirrors, water, glass)
Understanding flipped/mirrored images in design and printing

vocabulary.meaning: The left-right flipped version of something, as seen in a vertical mirror; left and right swap, top and bottom stay the same.
The top-bottom flipped version of something, as seen reflected in water below it; top and bottom swap, left and right stay the same.
A capital letter that looks exactly the same after a left-right flip: A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y.
A capital letter that looks exactly the same after a top-bottom flip: B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X.

story.title: The Word That Doesn't Change
story.text: Naina's grandmother holds up a card that says 'TOT' to a mirror. 'It still says TOT!' Naina says, surprised. Her grandmother explains: 'A mirror flips left-right. T and O are letters that look the same when flipped — and TOT reads the same forwards and backwards too, so both effects cancel out perfectly.' Then she holds up 'BOX' to the mirror — it looks completely garbled. 'B isn't mirror-symmetric,' her grandmother says, 'so as soon as one letter breaks the pattern, the whole word changes.'
story.extractedProblem: Does the word 'TOT' look identical in a mirror? Does the word 'BOX' look identical in a mirror?
story.answerInStory: TOT looks identical (all letters mirror-symmetric, and it's a palindrome); BOX does not (B is not mirror-symmetric).

visual.caption: TOT is built only from mirror-symmetric letters (T, O, T) and reads the same forwards and backwards — so its mirror image looks identical to the original.

teachingGallery.title: Water image: flips top-bottom, not left-right
teachingGallery.note: A water image keeps left-right order the same but flips every letter upside down. Only letters symmetric about a horizontal line (B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X) survive this unchanged.

examples.caption: HIKE is built only from water-symmetric letters (H, I, K, E) — its water image looks identical, just flipped upside down, with left-right order unchanged.

standardMethod.summary: For a MIRROR image: check if every letter is mirror-symmetric AND the word reads the same forwards and backwards (a palindrome) — both conditions are needed for the mirror image to look identical. For a WATER image: check if every letter is water-symmetric — left-right order never changes, so no palindrome check is needed.
steps: Identify whether the question asks for a mirror image (left-right flip) or a water image (top-bottom flip).
For mirror images: check each letter against the mirror-symmetric list (A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y), AND check if the word is a palindrome.
For water images: check each letter against the water-symmetric list (B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X) only — no palindrome check needed.
If every letter passes and (for mirrors) the palindrome check also passes, the flipped version looks identical to the original.
For clock times: use the mirror-time formula 11:60 minus the actual time.

alternateMethods.name: Clock mirror-time formula
alternateMethods.whenToUse: Questions asking what a clock's reflection in a mirror shows.
steps: Take the actual time shown on the clock.
Subtract it from 11:60 (treat this like 12:00, but written as 11:60 to make the subtraction easy without needing to borrow).
The result is exactly what the mirror image of the clock would show.
alternateMethods.example: Actual time 3:15 → 11:60 − 3:15 = 8:45. The mirror image of a clock showing 3:15 shows 8:45.

workedExamples.problem: Does the mirror image of the word 'MOM' look identical to the word itself?
steps: Check each letter for mirror symmetry: M is in the symmetric list (A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y). O is in the list too.
All letters (M, O, M) are mirror-symmetric.
Check if the word is a palindrome: MOM reversed is MOM — yes, it's a palindrome.
Both conditions pass, so the mirror image of MOM looks identical to MOM.
workedExamples.answer: Yes, MOM's mirror image looks identical to MOM

workedExamples.problem: A clock shows 4:20. What time does its mirror image show?
steps: Use the mirror-time formula: 11:60 minus the actual time.

trickPractice.trick: Mirror flips left-right AND reverses order; water flips top-bottom only
trickPractice.intro: Remember: a mirror image needs BOTH symmetric letters and a palindrome word; a water image only needs symmetric letters.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mixing up the mirror-symmetric letter list with the water-symmetric letter list — they overlap (H, I, O, X) but are not identical.
commonMistakes.fix: Mirror = left-right flip → A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y. Water = top-bottom flip → B,C,D,E,H,I,K,O,X. Memorize them as two separate lists that happen to share only a few letters.

commonMistakes.mistake: Checking only whether each letter is mirror-symmetric for a mirror-image word question, forgetting that the word's LETTER ORDER also reverses.
commonMistakes.fix: A mirror image needs BOTH: every letter individually symmetric, AND the whole word being a palindrome (reads the same forwards/backwards) — missing either check gives a wrong answer.

commonMistakes.mistake: Subtracting the actual time from 12:00 directly and getting a borrowing error, instead of using the cleaner 11:60 form.
commonMistakes.fix: Always rewrite 12:00 as 11:60 before subtracting — this avoids needing to 'borrow' an hour and keeps the minutes subtraction simple.

revisionCard.summary: Mirror image = left-right flip; needs every letter mirror-symmetric (A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y) AND the word to be a palindrome. Water image = top-bottom flip; needs every letter water-symmetric (B,C,D,E,H,I,K,O,X), with no palindrome check since left-right order never changes. Clock mirror times: subtract the actual time from 11:60.

rememberIt.hook: Mirror flips left-right + reverses order; water flips top-bottom only
rememberIt.unpack: Two different symmetric-letter lists, and only mirrors need the extra palindrome check.

studentQuestions.q: Why does a mirror image reverse the letter order but a water image doesn't?
studentQuestions.a: A mirror reflects left-to-right, so the letter that was on the right ends up appearing on the left (reversing order). A water reflection flips top-to-bottom only — nothing swaps left-right, so the order of letters stays exactly the same, just each one is upside down.

studentQuestions.q: Is there a quick way to remember the two letter lists?
studentQuestions.a: Notice the overlap: H, I, O, X appear in BOTH lists because they have a kind of 4-way symmetry. Learning those 4 first, then adding the rest to each list separately, is easier than memorizing two lists from scratch.
